I fixed the water temperature at 90°C, the coffee-to-water ratio, and the bloom time, and used three grind sizes—medium-coarse, medium-fine, and fine—to brew the same new beans. assistant.content: Your testing method is very scientific; fixing the variables and comparing one by one is a clear way to find the optimal grind size—great job! Regarding water temperature, 90°C is good for medium-dark roasted beans, but the optimal temperature for beans of different origins may fluctuate between 88 and 92°C. A coffee-to-water ratio of 1:15 is a common starting point, and light roasts can be adjusted to 1:16. For the pouring technique, I recommend using a small stream to draw concentric circles, keeping the kettle spout 2–3 cm above the water surface to avoid disturbing the coffee bed with too large a flow. I suggest recording your brewing notes to build a personal database. You can also check out 'Coffee Craftsman' or the advanced videos from Bilibili's 'Fragrant Coffee Journey.'

When pouring in circles, each pour should last 20-30 seconds, and keep the water surface steady during the intervals between pours. When practicing, you can record a video to review the water flow and note each flavor change. Compare a few times and you'll find your golden parameters. Looking forward to your next result!

user.content: I signed up for tomorrow evening's introductory pour-over coffee class and am pre-studying. Could you help me sort out the core parameters such as water temperature, grind size, and bloom time? And what exactly is the difference between a V60 and a cake dripper?

assistant.content: Key parameters: water temperature usually 88-94°C (higher for light roasts, lower for dark roasts); grind size similar to fine sugar; coffee-to-water ratio 1:15-1:17; blooming time 20-30 seconds. The V60 has fast flow and clear flavor layers; the cake cup has slow flow and is sweeter. I suggest you first focus on mastering pour stability and evenness.

user.content: Got it. So what mistakes are beginners most likely to make? For example, pour-over technique or grind size issues—I'd like to pay attention in advance to avoid them.

assistant.content: Common mistakes: water temperature too high leads to bitterness, grind too fine leads to over-extraction, and pouring too quickly leads to uneven extraction. Suggestions: practice pouring in circles with Bilibili videos in advance, buy a pour-over scale to control the amount of water, and after the bloom, wait for the coffee grounds to expand and stabilize before continuing to pour. The teacher may demonstrate these in class, so it will be more efficient to learn with your questions in mind.

These habits reinforced each other through the loop of experience → record → share → experience again: pour-over coffee became an inspiration trigger for camping and writing (outdoor pour-over on June 7, café exchange after writing class on June 14); writing and reading provided differentiated content for Xiaohongshu (family longtang stories, etc.); camping and pour-over gear were turned into Xiaohongshu content (filming camping gear on June 5, pour-over Vlog on June 8); A Fu's arrival not only increased family interaction, but also became new inspiration for writing and content (posted his video to Xiaohongshu on June 30). Together, these habits formed a multi-dimensional, organic life system.

user.content: I'm Lei Mingxuan, 31 years old, and it's my first time skiing. I've just got all my gear ready. I've watched some videos and learned the snowplow stop and basic stance, but I'm not confident, especially about falling safely and controlling speed. Can you give me a systematic set of beginner essentials and safety reminders?

assistant.content: Of course. The core is three parts: 1. Snowplow braking: lower your center of gravity, press both knees inward, open the ski tails into a V shape, and push snow with the inside edges of the skis to slow down. 2. Safe falling: when you feel out of control, actively fall sideways, fall toward the uphill side, and land on your elbows and hips, avoiding catching yourself with your hands or leaning back. 3. Speed control: always ski in a snowplow; on steep slopes, open the ski tails wider and use pole planting. I recommend starting on a green run (beginner slope) and avoiding peak hours.

user.content: How exactly do you perform a deliberate side fall? I'm afraid that if I don't fall correctly I'll get injured. Also, what mistakes are beginners prone to make when it comes to ski slope conduct?

assistant.content: Side fall: first bend your knees to lower your center of gravity, tilt your body toward the uphill side, and let the hip and shoulder on the same side touch the ground in sequence, keeping the skis together. Common mistakes: sitting back and injuring the tailbone, or bracing with your hands and causing a wrist fracture. Ski resort rules: don't stop in the middle of a trail or on a turn; leave enough distance when passing others; look uphill before entering a run. It is recommended to bring knee pads, hip pads, and ski goggles.

For training, you can add planks (3 sets per day, 45 seconds each) and one-legged standing stroke practice to strengthen balance. answer: In the physical fitness test on December 31, Lei Mingxuan successfully bench-pressed 50 kg (3 sets of 8 reps) and reached a 5 km treadmill pace of 5:50 per kilometer, achieving the goal set at the beginning of the month. These results were thanks to the progressive strength and aerobic training he had been doing since December 12: on December 12 he hired a personal trainer and customized a plan; on December 13, his first session, he bench-pressed 40 kg and ran at a pace of 6:00; on December 20 he still bench-pressed 40 kg but improved his pace to 5:30; on December 22 he bench-pressed 50 kg and ran at 5:20; on December 29 he bench-pressed 57.5 kg and ran at 4:50. By gradually increasing the weight and improving the pace in each session, the cumulative training effect allowed him to steadily hit his goal in the end-of-month test.

user.content: This afternoon I did squats at 67.5 kg, deadlifts at 77.5 kg, and bench presses at 57.5 kg, then ran for 50 minutes at a 4:50 per kilometer pace. The back of my thighs feels especially sore, possibly combined with fatigue from the weekend camping. Is this soreness a normal training response or a warning sign of overtraining?

assistant.content: Given the intensity and the added camping fatigue, the soreness is more likely delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS), which is a normal reaction. However, you need to confirm whether it is accompanied by any sharp localized pain or joint discomfort—you only did 5 minutes of stretching, which doesn't feel sufficient, right? Also, have you tried a foam roller or other active recovery methods?

user.content: Yes, the stretching was insufficient, and I didn't use a foam roller. It just feels tight, with no stinging pain or joint issues.

assistant.content: It is recommended to gently roll the back of the thighs and buttocks with a foam roller tonight, avoiding tender points; arrange low-intensity cardio (such as brisk walking or jogging for 30 minutes) tomorrow or the day after to promote blood circulation, and pause leg strength training in the meantime. For diet, consume 20-30g of protein (such as whey protein or chicken breast) within 1 hour after training to aid recovery. Over the next week, reduce squat and deadlift volume by 20%, prioritize recovery, and consider breaking through a 70kg squat the week after next.
